intro: Debussy’s Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune, which Pierre Boulez said brought “new breath to the art of music”, opens with a solo flute. Paul Paray conducts the Detroit Symphony Orchestra in a recording made for Mercury in 1955.

sections.label: A · Flute alone, then the orchestra
sections.mNote: The flute’s phrase returns with new harmony each time.

sections.label: B · D♭ major melody, woodwinds then strings
sections.mNote: Woodwinds, then strings, play the broad melody in D♭ major.

sections.label: A′ · Flute theme returns over harp
sections.mNote: Opening tempo; harp arpeggios fill the earlier rests.

sections.label: Coda · Antique cymbals, E major
sections.mNote: The opening phrase returns, slower; the music ends in E major.

cues.title: Opening flute solo
cues.text: The flute plays alone, marked doux et expressif. It starts on C♯, descends to G and rises again, outlining a tritone, an interval that belongs to no key. Nothing sounds beneath it for three bars; in bar 4 the harp plays a glissando and the horns enter on an unresolved chord.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 1–4: solo flute, Très modéré, doux et expressif; harp and horns enter in bar 4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP14736-Debussy_-_Pr%C3%A9lude_%C3%A0_l%27apr%C3%A8s-midi_d%27un_faune_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Debussy’s programme note, 1894
cues.text: Debussy’s note for the first audience called the piece “a very free illustration of Mallarmé’s beautiful poem … a succession of scenes through which the desires and dreams of the faun pass in the heat of the afternoon.” In Mallarmé’s poem the faun wakes unsure whether the two nymphs he remembers were real.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s programme note for the 1894 première, quoted with the French original at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prélude_à_l'après-midi_d'un_faune; Mallarmé’s poem (1876).

cues.title: Orchestration without trumpets
cues.text: For much of the piece the strings play muted and divided into many parts around the woodwinds. There are no trumpets, trombones or timpani, and the only brass are four horns. The brightest colours come from three flutes, oboes, cor anglais, clarinets and two harps.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895): instrumentation, and string parts marked sourdines (muted) and divisés (divided).
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: First performance, 22 December 1894
cues.text: At the première, in the Salle d’Harcourt on 22 December 1894, the eighteen-year-old Georges Barrère played the flute solo. The audience demanded the whole piece again, and Gustave Doret conducted it a second time.
cues.evidence: Première, venue and conductor: IMSLP work page, https://imslp.org/wiki/Prélude_à_l'après-midi_d'un_faune,_CD_87_(Debussy,_Claude). Barrère as soloist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Barrère. The encore: Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/prelude-to-the-afternoon-of-a-faun

cues.title: Middle section in D♭ major
cues.text: The middle section is in D♭ major. Here the piece has its first long, broad melody. The woodwinds play it together over syncopated strings, then the strings take it over and carry it to the climax.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 55–78 (from p. 15); bars 51–54 prepare the new key. Pearson Edexcel analysis of the work, https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/A%20Level/Music/2013/Teaching%20and%20learning%20materials/Unit-3-5-Debussy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nijinsky’s ballet, 1912
cues.text: In May 1912 Nijinsky made the piece into a ballet for the Ballets Russes, with his dancers moving in profile like figures on a Greek vase; he danced the faun himself. The final gesture caused a scandal. The editor of Le Figaro spiked his own critic’s review and denounced the ballet on the front page.
cues.evidence: Première 29 May 1912, Théâtre du Châtelet; Gaston Calmette’s front-page article in Le Figaro replacing Robert Brussel’s review: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afternoon_of_a_Faun_(Nijinsky), citing Buckle, Nijinsky.

cues.title: Return of the flute theme
cues.text: At Mouvement du début (rehearsal 8, bar 79) the opening tempo returns, and the solo flute plays its opening phrase again. At the start the flute played alone. Here the harps play beneath it.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 8 (bar 79), p. 21: Mouvement du début, solo flute over harps and divided strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The conductor, Paul Paray
cues.text: Paul Paray, the conductor here, won the Prix de Rome in 1911, twenty-seven years after Debussy. He was music director of the Detroit Symphony from 1952 and made this recording there for Mercury’s Living Presence series.
cues.evidence: Paray’s Prix de Rome (1911, cantata Yanitza) and Detroit post: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Paray. Mercury MG 50101 label: https://archive.org/details/lp_ibria-la-mer-prelude-to-the-afternoon-of_paul-paray-claude-debussy-detroit-symphony

cues.title: Antique cymbals
cues.text: The flute phrase returns at a slower tempo, and the score asks for “more languor”. Two antique cymbals play here for the first time. These are small tuned brass discs, struck softly, sounding E and B.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 10 (p. 27): Dans le 1er mouvement avec plus de langueur; cymbales antiques in E and B.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mallarmé to Debussy, December 1894
cues.text: Mallarmé wrote to Debussy straight from the concert in December 1894: “The marvel! Your illustration of the Afternoon of a Faun, which presents no dissonance with my text, but goes much further, really, into nostalgia and into light.”
cues.evidence: Mallarmé to Debussy, December 1894; English text in Maurice Dumesnil, Claude Debussy, Master of Dreams (1940), p. 181.

cues.title: Final cadence in E major
cues.text: The cadence and final chord in bars 105–110 are in E major, a key the opening tritone avoids. The piece ends as quietly as it began.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 105–110: cadence and final chord in E major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Into D♭ major
transitions.from: A · Flute alone, then the orchestra
transitions.to: B · D♭ major melody, woodwinds then strings
transitions.how: Four bars on an A♭ chord, the dominant of D♭, prepare the change of key. At bar 55 the woodwinds begin the long D♭ melody together, over strings playing off the beat. The melody is laid out in long phrases, where the opening theme was short and winding.
transitions.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 51–55, p. 15; Pearson Edexcel analysis, bars 51–78.

transitions.title: The opening tempo returns
transitions.from: B · D♭ major melody, woodwinds then strings
transitions.to: A′ · Flute theme returns over harp
transitions.how: The D♭ melody thins out in the strings and slows. At rehearsal 8, marked Mouvement du début, the solo flute plays its first phrase again, now over harp arpeggios and held string chords.

transitions.title: Slower, with antique cymbals
transitions.from: A′ · Flute theme returns over harp
transitions.how: The score returns to the first tempo “with more languor” at rehearsal 10 (bar 94). The flute’s phrase comes back once more, the antique cymbals enter in E and B, and the harmony moves towards E major.
transitions.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 10 (p. 27) to the end, bars 94–110.

timeline.note: Harp glissando and horns answer the flute.
Woodwinds play the long D♭ melody over the strings.
The opening tempo: flute over harp and held strings.
An oboe phrase over soft horns and strings.
The flute’s phrase returns, with antique cymbals.
Quiet woodwind, harp, antique cymbals and pizzicato low strings at the close.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
